meta.desc.agora: B2B product designer · From MVP to product, AI-ready design systems. AgoraSquare: the working day of Rungis market wholesalers, from the first order to the accounting close. Three weeks in the field, 92% adoption according to AgoraSquare's management.
ag.hero.04: B2B product designer · From MVP to product, AI-ready design systemsSimplifying a wholesaler's day, from 3 am to closing time.
ag.hero.05: Lead UX/UI on an application that took Rungis wholesalers from paper notebooks to digital: order taking, customer solvency, electronic invoicing and accounting, on a tablet at the market and on a computer at the office.

ag.probleme.02: The world's largest wholesale market was running on notebooks
ag.probleme.03: The Rungis market is the beating heart of France's food supply. Yet wholesalers were still juggling Excel sheets, paper notebooks and ageing software. Orders came in by phone, customer solvency was judged by gut feeling, and invoicing was done by hand.
ag.probleme.04: In a trade where every minute counts and the goods are perishable, that lost time is paid for twice: in missed sales, and in unpaid invoices.
ag.probleme.30: An order taken over the phone at 4 am. Switch over to see what becomes of it.
ag.probleme.31: Five pain points, always the same
ag.probleme.33: Slow entry, frequent errors, no reliable record.
ag.probleme.35: Repeated unpaid invoices, for lack of financial information at the moment of sale.
ag.probleme.37: 2 to 3 hours a day, taken from the core of the job.
ag.probleme.39: Customers, stock and invoices spread across several tools.
ag.probleme.41: Bank reconciliations done by hand, painful closings.

ag.enquete.02: Three weeks at Rungis, by night
ag.enquete.03: No office interview would have shown what a Rungis aisle shows at 3 am: the cold, the fatigue, the busy hands, the phone ringing while a pallet truck is being loaded. I observed, ran in-depth interviews and followed the real flows, then calibrated the design on those volumes.
ag.enquete.04: weeks of immersion at the market
ag.enquete.09: Drag through the day, or use the arrow keys.
ag.enquete.19: Wholesalers work at night, in the cold, with their hands full. A screen has to be readable at a glance and usable with gloves on.
ag.enquete.20: What changes High contrast, 48 px minimum targets, a dark mode for the night.
ag.enquete.22: The phone rings, the notebook fills up
ag.enquete.23: Fast entry is vital: a missed order means perishable goods lost. Every call becomes a scribbled line.
ag.enquete.24: What changes The express order: 4 steps instead of 12, favourites and a typo-tolerant search.
ag.enquete.26: Delivering without knowing if you will be paid
ag.enquete.27: A customer's solvency is judged by gut feeling. Financial risk weighs on every delivery, and unpaid invoices keep coming back.
ag.enquete.28: What changes A real-time solvency score, shown before validating.
ag.enquete.30: Two to three hours of paperwork
ag.enquete.31: Copying out notebooks, calculating, printing invoices: at least 2 to 3 hours a day, taken from the trade.
ag.enquete.32: What changes An electronic invoice generated in 3 steps, straight from the order.
ag.enquete.35: Without an overview, late payments are spotted too late. Reminders go out case by case, whenever someone thinks of it.
ag.enquete.36: What changes The aged balance, monitoring alerts and a reminder in one tap.
ag.enquete.39: Bank reconciliation and accounting remain approximate, and the market network often drops.
ag.enquete.40: What changes Offline sync and direct export to EBP, Sage or Cegid.
ag.enquete.41: Six findings that guided every decision
ag.enquete.43: From 3 am, in the cold and fatigue.
ag.enquete.47: Without visibility on solvency, unpaid invoices pile up.
ag.enquete.49: At least 2 to 3 hours of invoicing a day.
ag.enquete.51: No unnecessary feature that would slow things down.
ag.enquete.53: Frequent outages: a real offline mode is a must.
ag.enquete.56: A fruit and vegetable wholesaler for 25 years, one of the three personas drawn from the research. His goal: process orders fast, to sell more.
ag.enquete.57: “We need a fast, reliable tool. Here, every minute counts and we can't afford to waste time on a complicated system.”
ag.principes.03: The architecture follows the sales cycle, from order to accounting. Each module cuts the number of steps in the most frequent tasks, and the essential features open straight from the home screen.
ag.principes.09: Sell fast, even without a network. A 4-step express order, favourites for regular customers, a typo-tolerant search, purchase orders and delivery notes.
ag.principes.14: Know who you are selling to. A solvency score readable in under 3 seconds, the customer's average payment delay compared with their sector, and alerts when the score drops.
ag.principes.19: Invoice without thinking about it. Electronic invoices generated from the order, supplier invoices received by photo or text message, approval and payment.
ag.principes.24: Close the books without re-entering anything. Reconciled receipts, aged balance, cash flow by category, and export to the accounting software used at the market.
ag.principes.30: Three clicks at most for any action, and direct actions.
ag.principes.32: Real-time validation, clear messages, suggested corrections.
ag.principes.34: Strong hierarchy, colour-coded areas, high contrast.
ag.principes.36: Tablet and computer, touch targets of at least 48 px.
ag.principes.38: Everything works without a network; syncing happens when it comes back.
ag.principes.40: Every action responds right away, to reassure.
ag.principes.42: At the market, people tap fast, with cold fingers or gloves. Here, every tap wobbles a little, just like in the field. Hit the six buttons of each size, then compare.
ag.mesures.03: Timed during testing with 8 wholesalers, on scenarios kept identical from one session to the next: average times, varying with how busy the stand is. Switch between before and after.

ag.st1.03: On opening the app (with a code received by text message the first time), the wholesaler sees what lies ahead: invoices to check, to pay, to collect, and those that are overdue. Each tile opens its list directly.
ag.st1.04: DecisionThe essential features open from the home screen, with no menu to dig through: at 3 am, you want to know what to do.
ag.st1.11: opens in one tap, without going through a menu.
ag.st2.02: One call, one order in four steps
ag.st2.03: A restaurant owner calls. The wholesaler finds the customer in three letters, even mistyped, or with one tap in the favourites. The order fits in four steps and goes out even without a network.
ag.st2.04: Adjusted after testingFavourites for regular customers: they are one tap away, with no re-typing.

ag.st3.01: Step 3 · at the market · the check
ag.st3.02: Knowing whether you will be paid, before delivering
ag.st3.03: Before validating, the customer's solvency score appears, along with their average payment delay compared with their sector. The wholesaler decides with full knowledge: accept, ask for a deposit, or require payment with the order.
ag.st3.04: Validated in workshopsColour codes and interpretation messages tested in 3 workshops, for a reading in under 3 seconds.
ag.st3.intro: This customer pays faster than their sector: what do you decide?
ag.st3.17: Deposit requested, the order ships on receipt.
ag.st4.02: The delivery note is signed on screen
ag.st4.03: The order becomes a purchase order, approved in one tap. On delivery, the customer signs right on the tablet: no more paper slips to hunt for in the evening.
ag.st4.04: PrincipleImmediate feedback: as soon as it is signed, the note turns green and the invoice can go out.
ag.st4.12: Signature area: sign with your mouse or finger
ag.st5.02: An electronic invoice in three steps
ag.st5.03: The invoice is born from the delivery note: check, generate, send. Three steps instead of seven, and fifteen minutes brought down to three (average times, varying with how busy the stand is), in the electronic invoicing format.
ag.st5.04: Adjusted after testingThe invoicing flow went from 7 to 3 steps based on wholesalers' feedback.
ag.st5.intro: Check the amounts, then move on to the next step.
ag.st5.verified: Amounts checked: the electronic invoice can be generated.
ag.st5.18: Sent to the customer, and filed.
ag.st6.02: Supplier invoices come in on their own
ag.st6.03: They arrive through AgoraSquare, as a photo or a simple text message, then they are read, checked, approved or rejected, and finally paid. Each status has its own colour.
ag.st6.04: Adjusted after testingThe visual statuses were strengthened after misreadings during testing.
ag.st6.10: The supplier drops the invoice straight into your space.
ag.st6.11: A photo of the paper invoice, read automatically.
ag.st6.12: The supplier texts it to your dedicated number.
ag.st6.15: Approve the Primeurs du Val invoice

ag.st7.02: An expense claim is just a photo
ag.st7.03: The receipt is photographed, the amount and VAT are read, and the expense is filed in the right category. All that is left is to approve it.
ag.st7.04: PrincipleError prevention: whatever is read can still be corrected before validation.
ag.st8.02: See late payments, send a reminder in one tap
ag.st8.03: Customer payments are matched to invoices. The aged balance shows what is owed and since when, for customers and suppliers alike, and a reminder goes out without leaving the screen.
ag.st8.04: OutcomeAverage payment time brought down from 45 to 30 days, according to the heads of the equipped wholesalers.
ag.st8.label: Remind
ag.st9.03: AgoraSquare monitors the customer portfolio. When a score drops, an alert arrives before the next delivery, with the recommended action.
ag.st9.04: Outcome30% fewer unpaid invoices thanks to visibility on solvency, according to the heads of the equipped wholesalers.

ag.st11.02: The entries go to the accountant
ag.st11.03: At the end of the period, the entries are sent to the accounting software already in place: EBP, Sage or Cegid. No more re-entry, no more manual reconciliation.
ag.st11.04: Constraint metFit in with existing tools rather than replace them.
ag.st11.14: Entries exported, ready for the accountant.

ag.systeme.02: A design system for the night, the cold and gloves
ag.systeme.03: Every decision comes from a constraint seen in the field: readability in low light, generous touch areas, statuses understood at first glance.
ag.systeme.06: At least 16 px for body text, 24 px for headings. A contrast ratio of at least 7:1, for outdoor use.
ag.systeme.16: Green for paid or validated, orange for pending, red for blocked, on a light background that is easier on the eyes.
ag.systeme.27: A flexible grid, with spacing of at least 16 px to avoid off-target taps.
ag.systeme.32: One hand, 48 px targets, the main actions at the bottom of the screen for the thumb, and a dark mode for the night.
ag.systeme.33: Several columns, keyboard shortcuts for power users, sortable and filterable tables.
ag.systeme.35: Not requested at the start, built in anyway: AAA-level contrast, full keyboard navigation, labels for screen readers.

ag.lecons.07: Extended immersionThe 3 weeks at Rungis changed everything: no office interview would have revealed these constraints.
ag.lecons.08: Testing oftenEvery two weeks, with real users: many costly mistakes avoided.
ag.lecons.09: Co-creating from the startWholesalers involved early made the tool their own, which made adoption easier.
ag.lecons.10: Radical simplicityResisting “nice but not essential” features paid off.
ag.lecons.11: A design system from day oneIt sped up development and kept things consistent.
ag.lecons.12: Resistance to changeMany were attached to their notebooks. The answer: one-to-one support, training, and two weeks of double entry, on paper and digital.
ag.lecons.13: Offline, technically hardEspecially syncing. The answer: an architecture designed from the start with the CTO, and prototypes to check feasibility.
ag.lecons.14: Very different tradesFruit, meat, dairy: each with its own needs. The answer: flexible, configurable modules rather than one rigid block.
ag.lecons.15: Involve developers earlierSome ideas turned out to be complex to build: bringing them in at the wireframe stage would have saved back-and-forth.
ag.lecons.16: Plan more time for offlineSyncing took 30% longer than planned: the estimate should have been doubled.
ag.lecons.17: Document decisionsSome, made during the research, had been forgotten six months later.
ag.lecons.18: Anticipate how the product will evolveA few architecture choices slowed down adding features.
ag.lecons.19: Prepare training from the design stageIt was improvised: a programme planned early would have made adoption easier.
ag.lecons.20: Good design is not measured by its beauty, but by its impact on people's everyday lives. Seeing wholesalers save time and work with less stress was the best validation of this approach.
ag.faq.03: How long did the project last?
ag.faq.04: Eight months, from February to October 2022: field research (3 weeks), design, testing, development and a gradual rollout.
ag.faq.05: How was the research carried out?
ag.faq.06: Three weeks of immersion at Rungis: 15 wholesalers observed, 20 semi-structured interviews, 8 critical flows mapped.
ag.faq.08: The network often drops at the market. The application keeps working and syncs everything as soon as the connection is back.
ag.faq.10: Admin time cut from 3 h to 0.8 h a day (timed). 92% adoption among the first 25 wholesalers equipped, according to AgoraSquare's management. 30% fewer unpaid invoices and payment time down from 45 to 30 days, according to the heads of the equipped wholesalers.
ag.end.01: A business tool that needs to be simple?
ag.end.02: I help teams design B2B platforms that are reliable, accessible and built for the field. Open to freelance work, embedded support or focused missions.
